hops.afterHeading: How do you learn a cell's ancestry?
hops.title: A calico cat is a fate map you can see
hops.text: Look at the orange and dark patches on a calico or tortoiseshell cat. The orange coat variant sits on the X chromosome, so a female can carry orange on one X and dark on the other. Early in development, the cells that will become the coat's pigment cells randomly inactivate one X and pass that choice on as they divide. As those cells spread across the growing skin, clones that kept the same X active form patches of the same color. The white areas come from a separate gene. The X choice is permanent and inherited by daughter cells, which is the property Cre fate mapping builds on purpose.

sources.citation: Kaelin CB et al., Curr Biol 35(12):2826-2836.e5 (2025)
Ballouz S et al., Nat Commun 14(1):7226 (2023)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A calico cat with distinct orange, black and white patches lying on a sunny wooden windowsill beside a potted fern.
image.caption: Orange and dark patches show which X stayed active in each pigment-cell clone, a fate map nobody engineered.

hops.title: Bomb-test carbon dated human microglia
hops.text: The mouse fate map traces where microglia came from, but it cannot say how long a human microglial cell lasts. That takes a different kind of clock. In 2017, Jonas Frisén's group used one set by Cold War nuclear testing. The bomb tests raised atmospheric carbon-14, and new DNA takes up carbon from food, so it carries roughly the carbon-14 level of the time it was made. Dating cortical microglia from people born across six decades gave a median renewal rate of 28 percent per year and an average cell age of 4.2 years. Their model suggested some microglia last more than two decades.

sources.citation: Réu P et al., Cell Rep 20(4):779-784 (2017)
Réu P et al., Cell Rep 20(4):779-784 (2017)

image.caption: Bomb-test carbon-14 showed healthy adult cortical microglia average 4.2 years old, with a median renewal of 28 percent yearly.

hops.afterHeading: Schwann cells come from the crest, in steps
hops.title: In mice, many adrenal chromaffin cells start as Schwann cell precursors
hops.text: When a car horn blares behind you, the adrenaline that reaches your blood comes mainly from chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla. Embryologists long thought these cells came straight from migrating neural crest. In 2017, fate mapping in mice showed that large numbers of them take a detour. They start as Schwann cell precursors riding along the embryonic visceral motor nerve. At the forming adrenal gland they detach from the nerve, turn down Schwann cell precursor genes and switch on the chromaffin program. In mice, then, many of the cells that make fight-or-flight hormones began on the glial path.
